v: Sharmaaaa… Varmaaaaa… manakenti ee KHARMA!!! An inspired story needed sharper screenplay and direction; instead even a few Trivikram-mark dialogues lose their value inside a film that turns PK’s quirks into complete overkill.
e: Agnyaathavaasi frustrated me because even if the core story was familiar, the screenplay and direction still had every opportunity to make it work. A few trademark Trivikram lines survive, but weak staging drains their impact, while Pawan Kalyan’s deliberately eccentric performance is stretched so far that what might have been fun in one scene becomes exhausting across a full film.
body:
If the story itself is already inspired or familiar, then at the very least the screenplay and direction have to carry the film.

That is exactly where Agnyaathavaasi collapsed for me.

There are still a few trademark Trivikram dialogues, but the direction is so weak around them that even those lines lose much of their value.

Pawan Kalyan has a certain exaggerated, quirky performance style that fans can enjoy enormously when used in the right scene.

But if you stretch the same behaviour across an entire movie, what is charming for a few minutes can become complete overkill.

In Trivikram style, if I have to summarise my reaction to the film:

“Sharmaaaa… Varmaaaaa… manakenti ee KHARMA!!!!!” 😄

P.S. There was an aunty sitting behind me who laughed and shouted loudly through practically every scene and irritated me throughout the film — maybe the Jabardasth effect? 😛

Then the movie ended and she herself declared that it had no head or tail and was terrible.

After surviving the movie, I first wanted to ask her why she had tortured the rest of us for the entire runtime 😄

v: Salman the BHAI can carry routine films on sheer screen presence; Tubelight needed Salman the ACTOR to disappear into Laxman. That casting mismatch exposes every script weakness instead of hiding it.
e: Tubelight asks Salman Khan to carry an offbeat emotional story through innocence, childishness and vulnerability rather than star power. I respect his wholehearted effort, but Kabir Khan’s casting never convinced me: fans struggle to accept Bhai as a fragile ‘Tubelight,’ while neutral viewers struggle to forget Bhai long enough to believe the character.
body:
Salman Khan the BHAI can earn hundreds of crores even with mediocre, routine subjects simply because his screen presence is powerful enough to carry films like Dabangg, Ready or Prem Ratan Dhan Payo.

But that does not automatically mean Salman Khan the ACTOR can make every offbeat script work when the entire movie depends on his acting fitting a very specific character.

Bajrangi Bhaijaan had a strong storyline packed with different emotions and did not rely only on Salman’s acting range.

His enormous screen presence simply elevated already-strong material into a blockbuster.

Tubelight is different.

The script depends heavily on Laxman’s innocence, emotional bonding and childishness.

And that is exactly where I felt Kabir Khan failed in casting Salman.

With such a massive star inside the role, the (tube)light gets thrown directly onto the script’s loopholes instead of keeping them in the dark 😄

Full respect to Salman for the wholehearted effort he puts into becoming Laxman.

But there are certain performances where the actor has to disappear so completely that you forget everything you already know about the star.

For me, Salman never quite reaches that point here.

Bottom line: fans may not accept BHAI being a Tubelight, and regular audiences may struggle to digest Tubelight being played by BHAI!!!!!

v: The Godfather formula is beaten to death and Sarkar 3 brings no new WOW factor — but taken without impossible RGV expectations, the philosophical lines, Nagre aura, weird angles and Govinda BGM still make a serviceable return to familiar territory.
e: Sarkar 3 suffers mainly because both the genre and Subhash Nagre’s world have become deeply familiar. RGV does not reinvent the formula, so viewers expecting another landmark are bound to be disappointed; still, the film contains all the genre ingredients and felt to me like a filmmaker who had not reached home again, but had at least rediscovered the road back.
body:
The biggest problem with the Godfather-style genre is that after a point the stories and characterisations become repetitive and predictable.

After the first Sarkar, so many filmmakers tried to exploit this kind of power-politics setup that the genre was practically beaten to death.

So when RGV himself returned to Sarkar, many of us naturally expected him to give the genre a completely new angle or definition.

Unfortunately, he does not.

And I think a lot of the negative reaction came from exactly that gap between the expectation attached to RGV and what the film actually delivers.

I would even argue that, taken exactly as it is, this same movie might have been received as a decent hit if RGV’s name had not carried such enormous expectations.

Sarkar 3 still contains practically every required ingredient: powerful and philosophical one-liners, sophisticated businessmen, corrupt politicians, slow camera movements, weird camera angles and our own Govinda… Govinda… Goooovinda!!!!!

RGV does directional justice to that familiar world.

But by the third film, we are already accustomed to Subhash Nagre’s black clothes, white beard, silent-killer stare and the Govinda BGM.

So the WOW factor we experienced when we first watched Sarkar is naturally missing.

For the previous few years, I felt RGV had lost much of his golden filmmaking touch from an audience perspective and had become far more visible through social-media controversies.

With Sarkar 3, I would not say he is completely back home.

But he has definitely found the road back.

P.S. After spending so many years experimenting with slow motion, camera angles and different kinds of cameras, I really hope RGV now uncovers something genuinely new in filmmaking and storytelling that can once again make both audiences and filmmakers go AWE!!!!!

v: Rajamouli playing completely to his strengths — ELEVATIONS, EMOTIONS and Keeravani’s deadly BGM!!! Devasena and Bhallaladeva become the pillars, Rana is terrific, and even supporting characters get full-impact hero moments.
e: Baahubali 2 doubles down on everything Rajamouli does best: emotional payoff, larger-than-life elevations and brilliantly staged action powered by M.M. Keeravani’s score. Anushka’s Devasena and Rana’s Bhallaladeva dominate the concluding chapter, while the story takes centre stage strongly enough to answer anyone who felt the first film’s spectacle overshadowed its narrative.
body:
Rajamouli plays completely to his strengths!!!!!

Those elevation scenes… those emotions… and then Keeravani’s deadly BGM on top of them 🙏🙏

The man even gives a supporting character like Subbaraju a couple of proper elevation shots and somehow creates full impact.

Anushka as Devasena and Rana as Bhallaladeva are the two pillars of this concluding part.

Rana is terrific, especially through his expressions.

There are moments around Baahubali’s death where the look on his face alone carries enormous weight 🙏🙏

After watching the first part, I expected Sivagami’s character to dominate the sequel.

Instead, Rajamouli makes Devasena even more powerful and almost tells Sivagami, “Papa, pakkaki velli aadukommaaa” 😄

I used to think only Sukumar could make even title cards feel creatively special, but Rajamouli proved me wrong here too.

Logic can obviously be kept aside during some of the fights, but the action is staged TERRIFICALLY.

And after RGV’s Shiva, one of the most memorable uses of a chain inside a fight sequence for me came again in this climax 🙂

Some people complained after the first film that graphics dominated the story.

Then the second film arrived with story and emotion dominating the graphics, and somehow a few people managed to complain about that too 😄

Meeru elli dubbing cinemalu chusukondi poyi!!!!!
